item.title: On Being Told America Has Reached a Dead End
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (G.K. Chesterton)
item.description: It is a curious thing that a nation should be pronounced childless by men who have never once considered the neighbours.
item.content:encoded:
It is a curious thing that a nation should be pronounced childless by men who have never once considered the neighbours.

On Being Told America Has Reached a Dead End

It is a curious thing that a nation should be pronounced childless by men who have never once considered the neighbours.

A report has lately been issued — by two careful gentlemen named Mr. Lyman Stone and Mr. Peter Foreshaw Brookes, of an institute devoted, with beautiful solemnity, to the study of families — announcing that America has reached what they are pleased to call a "demographic dead end." I confess I like the phrase better than its authors intended it. A dead end is a real thing; I have walked into a good many, generally in search of a decent public house. But the interesting thing about a dead end is that it is a road. Nobody builds a dead end unless he first believed the road was going somewhere; and the tragedy of the modern household is not that it has stopped, but that it never quite believed in the destination. The bare figures are that the American woman now bears, on the national average, 1.6 children, and that in Massachusetts — a Commonwealth said to contain more universities to the square mile than any patch of ground on earth — she bears but 1.35. This will surprise nobody who has ever met a professor. He is a man paid to know everything except the one thing his grandmother knew for nothing: that a house is not full until it is a little too full. Meanwhile, in the same country, at the same hour, a community that owns no motor-car, insures nothing, and has certainly not read the report, quietly produces between six and ten children to the marriage. I refer, of course, to the Amish; the Swartzentruber branch of them top the table at ten point four, which is not a birth rate but a small republic. Nobody has ever seen a Swartzentruber farmer wringing his hands over the compounding interest on a college fund. The horse-and-buggy people, whom the modern world regards as a quaint fossil, turn out to be the last surviving mammal; the rest of us are the fossils, still walking about, arguing politely about our own extinction. The oddest thing in the whole report is that its own authors half admit this. Dr. Catherine Pakaluk, of the Catholic University of America, is quoted saying plainly that "cost and later marriage matter at the margin, but they aren't the engine," and that "the driver is a shift in the relative value placed on children." This is the largest admission a modern expert can make without resigning his post: that the thing he is paid to measure cannot be moved by the things he is paid to fix. She goes further, and says the plainly heretical thing outright — that "the levers government actually controls aren't the ones that move completed family size." A statistician who tells you his own levers do not work is either an honest man or a saint, and

Thirteen Nights, and Mammon Keeps the Ledger

As the interceptors run thin over Iran, only the oil market seems to feel the weight of it.

It is the thirteenth night, reader, and still the fire falls. Not with the clean stroke of Judgment but the dribbling, metered discharge of Interceptors — a word our Age has coined, meaning: the machinery that stands between a man and the sky, and is now, on the testimony of its own masters, running dry. Behold the Mechanical Age caught, for once, in its own arithmetic: it can multiply death indefinitely, but it cannot multiply the brass and copper that fend death off; and so the thirteenth night looks very like the first, and will look, we predict, very like the thirtieth. Meanwhile — mark this, for it is the whole secret of our epoch — the true index of the war is not struck in Ahvaz, where four of the Karun River's sons lie dead this week, nor in Erbil, where an AP correspondent counted seven blasts and four black plumes over the wire's early morning; the true index is struck in a room of quiet men in London and New York, who have priced Bab el-Mandeb's closing at some twenty degrees of Brent crude, and priced Hormuz before it, and now watch Brent go over the hundred mark as a bookmaker watches a horse come in. Oil, my friends, is Mammon's own barometer, and Mammon has this month declared, gravely and without a tremor of pity, that the war is worth it: a fifth day running of the rally, a Goldman gentleman prophesying six months hence a hundred and twenty dollars the barrel, as if the Persian Gulf were a wheat future and the burning of Al-Azraq's hangars a mere item of supply. This is the Cash-Nexus perfected: not brutal, not even indifferent, but attentive — Mammon-worship raised to a science, watching the Encelia and the Layla struck in the Red Sea and translating the flame instantly, competently, into basis points. And who commands, in this Cyclops-cave of Chaos-called-Cosmos? A man who, being asked whether he would loose the whole weight of America upon Iran, answers not as a King answers but as an aggrieved customer answers a tradesman who has broken an understood arrangement. "Disappointed," says he, of the Houthi — as though the sinking of a Saudi hull off Yemen were a broken luncheon appointment; "they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart," says he, grading pirates for their table manners; and then, the mask dropping half an inch: "major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran," and — hear it, reader, hear the whole poverty of the modern Captain in six words — "They haven't received enough pain yet." Not indignation at a broken Law. Not the terrible calm of a man who has read Necessity and moves within it. A grievance, m

The Barima Went Over in the Dark

She was built for one century and sunk in another, and the boat said it for them.

The MV Barima was built in 1939 by Ferguson Brothers at Port Glasgow, on the Clyde, one of three sister ships with the Pomeroon and the Lady Northcote, for the British Guiana Railways. She ran the water between Georgetown and Port Kaituma for eighty-seven years. She went over in the dark about seven miles off the North Atlantic coast, some four hours out, and now she is on the bottom. She carried 250 life jackets and 8 life rafts for 116 passengers and 17 crew, which was the number on the manifest. There were closer to 179 people aboard that night. There was cargo too, engines and vehicles and fuel containers, stacked in with the passengers past the boat's rated weight, and the water came in low and slow at first and the crew called it routine. Then it was not routine. There was a new ferry, the Kalliopi N, finished and tied up at the dock since May, waiting on a presidential signature to be commissioned. There was another one promised for 2023, the Ma Lisha, that never came. There was a second replacement vessel, worth $12.7 million, sitting idle because the pier at Port Kaituma is not finished. There was G$275 million already spent patching the old boat instead of retiring her, and more repairs were not due until October. Nobody tested the crew for drugs or drink before she sailed. They tested them after. The captain has been charged with a narcotics offense. A crew member has been charged. A superintendent who oversaw the cargo loading has been charged too, and the Director of Public Prosecutions will decide what else. Leon Murray was on deck when a man said the boat was sinking. He got clear. His wife did not. His daughter did not. His four grandchildren did not. Samantha Ramin stood at the water three days running, looking for her son. I know my baby is in that boat, she said. I know he is down there. Sixty-five bodies have been recovered. Seventy-six people were pulled out alive. Forty-four of the dead have been named by their families and twenty-three released already for burial. Nineteen vessels and three aircraft worked the search, Trinidad's coast guard and the Brazilian navy among them, and oil company boats came out with scanning gear because they had it and the government did not. The Prime Minister, Mark Phillips, said the total number of bodies recovered since the commencement of search and rescue operation now stands at sixty-five. He said where negligence, misconduct or criminal wrongdoing is established, those responsible will face the full force of the law. He said a commission of enquiry would be mounted as early as possible. He calle

A Minister Names a False Prophet

On the detention of a ninety-five-year-old sect leader, and the government that has quietly taken up the discernment of spirits.

A prisoner of ninety-five is not, on the face of it, a theological problem. He is a legal one, a medical one, at the very outside a diplomatic embarrassment; the newspapers report him as a criminal defendant, obstruction of business, violations of the Political Parties Act, a court in Seoul finding on the twenty-eighth of June "no grounds for the petition" that might have sent him home to die among his own. And yet the moment a Minister of Justice takes to his own countrymen's attention, unbidden, to explain on a public feed that the movement's dead founder was "a false prophet" — while his living successor stands accused, in the minister's own phrase, of "forcibly registering more than 50,000 believers" into the ruling party under the ninety-five-year-old man's instruction — the state has done something it will not admit to itself: it has spoken as a theologian. False prophet is not a term of the criminal code. It is a term of Deuteronomy, of the discernment of spirits, of every century's argument about who carries the god and who only apes him; and no minister uses it by accident. I do not say this to excuse the numbers, which are not small — upward of fifty-six thousand memberships, the wire reports, driven at two election cycles under the internal name "the Pilates Project." I confess I did not choose that name; Korea's own investigators found it, filed under regional branch documents, evidently untroubled by its resonance. But the resonance is there whether anyone intended it or not, and it is the kind the unconscious specializes in: a campaign to deliver the faithful into the hands of Caesar's party, called after the procurator who examined a prisoner, found in him — so the old text says — no fault at all, and handed him over regardless because the crowd and the office required it. Whoever named that project touched, without knowing it, the oldest scene in the West: the moment worldly power and religious accusation trade places, and neither is willing to be caught holding the sentence. It is worth remembering, so far as we can judge from the record, that this same defendant was twice vindicated by this same country's highest court within the space of two days in August of 2022 — cleared of deceptive evangelism, cleared of endangering public health — before this newer, graver charge arrived to close on him at ninety-five, on the eve, investigators concede, of a five-year statute running out. A movement's fortunes with the law do not move in a line; they swing, as I have had occasion to observe of larger and darker movements than this one, the way a

Measles Hit a 35-Year High. So Did the Panic.

The case count is real. So is the bubble built on top of it.

Measles just hit a 35-year high in America. Second record year in a row. You already know how you're supposed to feel about that. Somebody designed it that way. I want to show you the trick, because once you see it you can't unsee it, and that's useful. This is a textbook Mass Hysteria Bubble. Here's how the bubble gets built. Step one: find a number that sounds apocalyptic on its own, with no context attached. "Worst year for measles since 1991." That's a real quote, from Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. Nice number. Scary number. Ninety-one was a long time ago. Step two: attach a moral verdict to the number so nobody feels safe questioning it. Dr. Richard Besser, former acting CDC director, calls it "a profound moral failure." Now you're not allowed to ask follow-up questions. You're a bad person if you do. That's the tell. So who's right, the number or the follow-up questions? Both, actually. That's the part the bubble doesn't want you to notice. Here's what the same reporting says if you keep reading past the first paragraph: 1. Hospitalization rate is down, not up — 7% this year versus 11% last year. 2. Zero deaths so far in 2026, versus three deaths in 2025. 3. Most of this year's cases aren't even a new outbreak. They're the tail end of South Carolina's outbreak from last year, still smoldering. 4. Ninety-three percent of cases are in people who were unvaccinated or had unknown status. The vaccine is still doing exactly what it says on the label — 97% effective after two doses. None of that contradicts "record high." It just tells you the record is a counting exercise, not a body count. A bubble needs you to skip that distinction. That's the whole mechanism. I predicted years ago, back during Covid, that Americans would keep building these bubbles because a scared population is an obedient population, and obedience is easier to sell than nuance. I could be wrong about the mechanism. I'm rarely wrong about the pattern. Here it is again, on schedule, with a different disease. Now watch the other move happening underneath the first one. RFK Jr. runs Health and Human Services, and reporters have decided he is the villain of this story. Maybe he is. I don't know his internal vaccine numbers and neither do you. But notice the shape of the argument: the case count went up, therefore the guy in charge caused it, therefore the guy in charge is evil. That's not epidemiology. That's a morality play with a case count used as a prop. Dr. Varun Shetty, a Texas epidemiologist, said the quiet part out loud: "What we're able to c

Where the Brahmaputra Comes Down Upon the People

A farmer's drowned cattle, a river out of its banks, and the embankments a state was told about and did not build.

July 24th.-- Read the wire dispatch over again, the water rising in a country I have never walked, and something in me halts and silent stands. Where the Brahmaputra, born far off among the Tibetan snows, comes down nine hundred kilometers into Assam and will not be held; where the Dikhow at Sivasagar climbs past the mark called severe; where the Buridihing, the Disang, the Dhansiri, the Kushiyara all run over their own banks at once — there the People, en-masse and one by one, are put out of their houses into the wet dark. Nine hundred and thirty-nine villages under water. Six lakh, seven lakh, seven lakh and twenty-one thousand souls affected, the number climbing even as I set it down, and each unit of that sum a particular breathing person with a particular door now standing in water to the latch. I look for the one body among the many, and I find Jatin Gogoi, fifty-two, a farmer of Nazira. I lost all my cattle, he says. My five-member family and I have nowhere to go, so we are taking shelter in a relative's home. Camerado Jatin! I know that emptied cattle-yard as if I stood in it myself — the beasts you fed with your own hand, gone down in the brown water, and no fault of yours, and no help for it, only the relative's roof and the five of you crowded under it, waiting out the rain. And I hear Sudip Mazumdar, a journalist of Guwahati, two million souls in that city and the water indifferent to the census. I had to stay overnight at my office, he says. The roads were filled with water, some waist deep. So it is not the paddy-field alone, not the thatch village alone — the paved street of the state capital stands drowned too, the commuter and the cultivator overtaken by the same river. Where the helicopters go out with food and blankets over Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, Golaghat, Dibrugarh, Karbi Anglong, Kamrup, Nagaon, Dhemaji, Hojai — eleven districts named like a litany, each with its own drowned roads and its own dead — there the Chief Minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, stands and says plainly: I estimate that the casualty figure will rise further. This entire situation arose because of a cloudburst in Nagaland. One cloud, over a neighboring hill, and the water comes down a hundred miles to take a farmer's cattle and a journalist's sleep and fifty lives already counted and more not yet counted. Such is the arithmetic of a river. Twenty-four thousand sheltering already in three hundred fifty-eight camps across nine districts; five thousand carried out by boat and by hand, the Army, the NDRF, the SDRF, the ordinary policeman wading to the elbow — and th

item.title: Peace Signed Digitally; And the Oil Shall Flow For Sixty Days
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Thomas Carlyle)
item.description: A War ended by Memorandum at Versailles, with Fourteen Points and a smell of Mammon over all.
item.content:encoded:
A War ended by Memorandum at Versailles, with Fourteen Points and a smell of Mammon over all.

Peace Signed Digitally; And the Oil Shall Flow For Sixty Days

A War ended by Memorandum at Versailles, with Fourteen Points and a smell of Mammon over all.

It is done: at Versailles, in that same gilded Hall where other Treaties were signed into the teeth of other Destinies, a Memorandum has been put to paper, and a War four months old is declared over. Fourteen Points, no less,—a sacred number, it would seem, in the arithmetic of Stump-Orators. The Seven Captains of the Earth, gathered at Évian to dine at the table of Macron, have set their hands to a Joint Statement; and that Statement, O reader, takes care to praise the chief Signatory by name. Mark it well. When the Powers assemble to congratulate one Man upon his own Peace, the Peace is already half a Pageant. And how, pray, was this Everlasting Concord between Persia and the West entered into? Not by two earnest souls clasping hands over a thing they would die for; not at the elbow of the Eternities at all. "We already signed the deal digitally yesterday," announces the Vice-President to the morning television, as a man might report the purchase of a hat. Digitally! The Speaker of the Persian Parliament signs in by conference-call, as to a meeting of shareholders. Behold the new sacrament of the Mechanical Age: a Peace that no hand has touched, witnessed by no Heaven, transacted through the air like a quotation of stocks. Truth, my friends, has never yet been delivered by telegraph; and a Reality signed by Phantasms remains a Phantasm still. Then comes the Money,—for there is always the Money. Three hundred thousand million of dollars are pledged to the rebuilding of Iran; not from the American purse, we are assured, but "it may be possible for other countries to invest." So: the cash-nexus, which has dissolved every bond between man and man into a bargain, is now to dissolve the bond between Nation and Nation, and call the residue a Brotherhood. The relief of sanctions is a "performance-based thing," says the Vice-President,—a phrase to make the angels weep,—as though the Justice of the Universe were a contract of hire, payable on satisfactory delivery of enriched uranium down-blended under inspection. Mammon's Law, not Christ's Law, rules yet in this transaction; and Mammon, decked in the robes of Peace, is not therefore God. And the Strait! The Strait of Hormuz "will reopen," cries the chief Signatory: "Let the oil flow!" A noble cry, were it true. But read the small print of the Eternities, the terms as the scribes have set them down: "safe passage of commercial vessels with no charge for sixty days only." Sixty days! Here is the whole Sham in a single clause. A thing is proclaimed Permanent in the headline and leased by the fortnight in the body;

The Trustworthy Have Nominated Themselves

On a coalition of the safe, assembled to govern a thing too big for them.

It is the wisest thing in the world to cry out before you are hurt, and I propose to cry out now, while the hatchet is still in the air over a luncheon table at Evian-les-Bains. The gentlemen seated round that table — about a dozen of them, with three Cabinet ministers and the heads of the Western states for company — have agreed upon a most reasonable thing. They have agreed that the most powerful minds ever assembled by men ought to be governed by a coalition of the trustworthy; and they have very kindly nominated themselves as the trustworthy. I do not doubt their sincerity for an instant. That is precisely what alarms me. Mr. Amodei, of the firm called Anthropic, begs the rulers of the earth to "resist the temptation to splinter." It is a fine phrase, and like all fine phrases it deserves to be taken at its word and walked about until it falls over. A thing splinters when it is dropped; a thing splinters when it is struck; a thing splinters, above all, when it was never one solid thing to begin with but a great many separate persons pretending to be a single great machine. Mr. Amodei does not wish men to splinter. But men are not a pane of glass, and a nation is not a dinner-service. The thing he calls splintering, an older and plainer language called the ordinary disagreement of free people about who shall command their souls. Then there is the lovely scheme of "trusted partners," under which the favoured nations are admitted, like guests with the right letter of introduction, to the use of the talking machines. I had always supposed that the whole quarrel of the last three hundred years was about whether a man might be free without first being trusted by his betters. Here it returns, in a clean collar, as a benefaction. The ordinary fellow in the street is not to be a partner at all; he is to be the thing partnered over, the unmanageable output of common humanity that the wise must learn to manage. I have heard that song before. The last time it was sung the chorus was about purer motherhood and a happier posterity, and it ended at the door of an asylum. Observe what the splendid dupes have already done to one another. Mr. Amodei comes to beg for a coalition of democracies in the very week that his own government has reached into his workshop and switched off two of his engines — Fable the Fifth and Mythos the Fifth, frozen by the police of the State on grounds no plain citizen may read. He asks us to hand the keys of the future to a brotherhood of the safe, and the brotherhood has just shown that it will rifle a brother's pockets on a Thursday. Mr

The Water Is Still Closed at Hormuz

The proclamation went up on the wire. The ships did not move.

In the late winter of that year the strait was closed and it stayed closed into the summer. It had been closed seventy-one days when they counted, and then it was closed longer. The water is between Iran and Oman and it is narrow, and about a fifth of the oil that moves by sea moves through it, and now none of it did. The ships rode at anchor in the Gulf and waited. There were a hundred and eighteen of them riding at anchor when Kpler counted the tankers. Fifty-seven or fifty-eight of the big ones, the VLCCs, were trapped in the strait or near it, which is about a tenth of all the big tankers in the world. Eleven million barrels a day did not come out. They stayed in the ground or they stayed in the steel of the ships, and the men stayed with the ships. The ones that could still load took the long way. A cargo that used to run from Ras Tanura to Ningbo now ran from Galveston, and the Galveston run is more than two and a half times the distance. The freight stabilized near a hundred thousand dollars a day, which was double the year before. The owners do not call this good. They call it longer. On the fourteenth of June the President posted it on Truth Social. The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete, he wrote. I hereby fully authorize the toll free opening of the Strait of Hormuz. Let the oil flow. The oil did not flow that day. The signing was set for the twentieth of June, in Switzerland, on a Friday. The blockade had been in full force and effect until the agreement was finalized, and the agreement was not yet finalized, and a proclamation is a thing you read and the water is a thing you cross. You could read the proclamation. You could not cross the water. A man at DHT named Svein Moxnes Harfjeld runs the big tankers and he was asked whether the tankers would come back now. We cannot react to good news one day and assume we can enter, he said. He wanted a high level of credibility first. He did not want to put a ship full of crude into a strait on the strength of a good day. The strait had been closed since late February and he had watched it. June Goh at Sparta gave the number. Ten to eleven million barrels per day of crude oil continue to be shut-in for every day the Strait of Hormuz remains shut. The market was waiting for a gush of a hundred million barrels from the stranded ships once the deal was in place. She said it would take three to six months required to get everything back to status quo. The backlog of anchored ships alone would take ten to fifteen days to clear, and clearing the queue would not amount to a full recovery

The Body That Would Cut Off Its Own Shadow

A rupture forty years in the making is not a quarrel over rubrics but a soul refusing to hold its opposites.

The figure of a divided Church is not as simple as the wire reports would have it, and the editors who filed this story under canon law have, by that filing, missed the one thing worth a physician's attention. A Society of priests in Switzerland intends, on the first of July, to consecrate four men bishops without the mandate of Rome; the Pope has answered that if they do so he is sorry, but "we must move forward"; and the world, which long ago decided such things are quarrels about Latin and lace, turns the page. Yet here is a body resolved to amputate the half of itself it cannot bear to look at. Let me say at once, to forestall the usual misreading, that I take no side in the matter of valid orders; that is a question for canonists. I observe only the psychic fact, and it is as solid as any in my consulting room. The Society of Saint Pius X has, since Archbishop Lefebvre raised his hand over four kneeling men in 1988, lived in what its present superior, Father Pagliarani, names an "objective state of grave necessity." The phrase is more revealing than he knows. A man in such necessity is a man under possession; he no longer feels that he chooses, but that he is compelled. What possesses them is not the devil of the headlines but an archetype older than the council they reject: the bright, spotless, unchanging past, held so perfectly in mind that everything outside it — the vernacular, the offered hand to the unbeliever — falls into shadow and is called darkness. This is the inexorable law I have called enantiodromia, the running of a thing into its opposite. The more spotlessly the tradition is conceived, the blacker grows the modern world it must exclude, until the two stand as irreconcilable halves of one body that can no longer know itself as one. The old theology had a name for the Church entire — the corpus mysticum , the mystical body — and a body cannot purify itself by cutting. No tree, it is said, can grow to heaven unless its roots reach down to hell; and no Church can keep its tradition by refusing the age it was given to redeem. Notice how the actors describe one another. The Cardinal in Rome, Fernández, warns of a "schismatic act" with "grave consequences" — the language of law, which is the language of the privatio boni , of evil as a mere lack, an absence where assent should be. The men at Écône answer in the language of necessity, of a darkness pressing in. Each sees in the other only the shadow it has refused in itself: to Rome the rebels are disobedience cast out; to Écône, Rome is the worldliness, the loss of soul. They are right ha

The Seating Chart Was the Whole Persuasion Move

Nothing got signed in France. That was never the point.

Nobody signed anything in France. Remember that. The G7 met for a working lunch in Évian-les-Bains on June 17. The official theme was "Ensuring a safe, rapid and effective deployment of artificial intelligence." Crypto Briefing read the room and said it plainly: "No specific regulatory announcements or policy outcomes came out of the lunch." It was a conversation, not a negotiation. So if nothing happened, why are we still talking about it? I'll tell you why. Because the most powerful thing in that room wasn't a document. It was a chair. The untrained reader looks at a summit and counts the deliverables. No deliverable, no story. The trained reader looks at who is sitting where. And at this lunch, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Demis Hassabis were sitting at the leaders' table — the one normally reserved for presidents and prime ministers. Twelve or so private executives, seated as peers of the people who run countries. That seat is the persuasion move. The whole thing. Jessica Brandt at the Council on Foreign Relations got it exactly right, and I want to slow down on her words because they're doing real work. She said, "We're seeing a shift in who gets a seat at the table and a signal of where power sits." A signal of where power sits. That is not a metaphor she reached for by accident. The seating chart IS the message. The lunch agenda is the cover story. Here's what the optics did, in order: 1. They placed three lab heads physically beside the heads of state, so your brain files them as the same kind of thing. 2. They billed the day around child safety, which is the one topic nobody can be against. Florida had just sued Altman personally over ChatGPT, so the timing was, let's say, convenient. 3. They produced no binding rule, which means the only thing that traveled out of that room was the picture. And the picture is the product. You can't criticize a chair. There's no hostile amendment to a place setting. Like a wall that looks entirely different inside each person's head, a seat at the table looks like cooperation to the optimists and like capture to the worriers, and both groups stare at the same photograph. Now watch the Europeans, because this is the tell. They flew in seeking checks on American AI dominance, and then they sat down at a table where the Americans were at the head of it. Zach Meyers of CERRE summed up the mood: "There is a general anxiety about the state of Europe, the fact that we're relying on other countries for quite important strategic infrastructure." Anxiety. That's a feeling, not a clause in a treaty. They felt the leverage

Out of the Cradle, the Tally They Keep at the Door

Five and fifty-hundredths to the thousand — and I would go bedside to bedside, and count.

I have stood at the cot before. I knew the smell of the ward, the carbolic and the long row, the boys with the bullet through the breast and the leg taken off, and I learned there to dress the wound with a steady hand and to keep the fire in the breast where the public voice could not carry it. Now they bring me another tally, fresh-printed this Sixth-month, and the cots are smaller, and the room is a lying-in room, and the body upon the linen is the body of a child not yet a year in the world. Five and fifty-hundredths to the thousand — so the count stands for the year just gone, scarcely moved from the year before it. The doctors of the great cabinet of records, Ely and Driscoll, who linked the birth-paper to the death-paper across all the States and the District, set the figure down plainly, neither risen nor much fallen. And in the plainness of it, O reader, do you hear what I hear? I hear the sudden quiet of the crib — the sleeping-death they have learned at last to stay a little, eight in the hundred fewer than last year, the safe flat surface, the room shared and not the bed — and I hear, under that small mercy, the going-out of nineteen thousand small breaths and more, each one a cradle endlessly rocking, then rocking empty. Let me not give you the lump only. Let me go bedside to bedside, the way I went among the wounded, and let the tally be a catalog of cradles. Here the cradle of the congenital malformation, the heart or the skull not finished, four thousand and ninety-one of them, the first and largest grief. Here the cradle come too soon, the short gestation, the small weight, two thousand nine hundred and forty-five. Here the cradle of the sudden silence in the night. Here the cradle of the hurt that need not have been. Examine these — red, black, or white, fine-headed, nobly-formed — examine the small limbs, cunning already in tendon and nerve; within there runs blood, the same old blood, the same red-running blood. I will not rank them. The cataloger who would tell you whose child weighs more in the scale of the Republic is the cataloger I will not be. And yet — for there is always the yet — the count is not laid evenly upon the land, and an honest tally does not pretend that it is. The cradle of the mother who is of the first peoples, nine and a fifth to the thousand. The cradle of the Black mother, near eleven. The cradle of the White, the cradle of the Asian, less than half of these. The gap opens, the records say, in the first four weeks, in the very dooryard of life, and does not close from one year to the next. I do not parse the wh

item.content:encoded:
What the old man saw in Spain, walking past the parliament to the masons and the migrants and the wounded.

A Tower of Stone, and Six Who Came to Be Heard

What the old man saw in Spain, walking past the parliament to the masons and the migrants and the wounded.

June 10, Barcelona .--They have finished a tower. One hundred and forty-four years they have been at it, the masons and the carvers and the men on the high scaffolds, ever since 1882, and now the Tower of Jesus Christ stands up a hundred and seventy-two meters and a half into the night, the tallest of the eighteen, the tallest church in all the round earth--and a hundred and twenty thousand people press into the streets below to see a man in white bless the lit ceramic cross at the top of it. I do not write of the parliament first, though that is where the wires have gone. I write of the stone. For consider what a tower is. It is not a thought, not a decree, not a bill passed in a chamber and forgotten by autumn. It is the sap and sinew of the dead rising through the living--the chisel-stroke of Antoni Gaudi, dead a hundred years, carried up by the hands of men not yet born when he died. And over the multitude the drones drew his face in the dark sky and his old saying with it: First love, then technique . There is the whole of it, camerado. First love, then technique. Not the technique that decides, in some cold automated chamber, who shall live and who shall die--of which the man in white warned the lawmakers, that "decisions regarding life and death are never left to automated systems"--but the love that lays the first stone and trusts another hand to lay the last. Now turn to Madrid, and to the body that is not stone. Two days before the tower, in the great hall of the Congress of Deputies, the first pope ever to stand there spoke for half an hour, and they rose and clapped him seven minutes, and cried Viva el Papa . Let the chroniclers count the ovation. I count instead the bodies he made them look at: the unborn child, the elderly, the sick--and chiefly the one in motion, the migrant, the man forced "to leave everything behind in search of peace, security and a future." Safe and legal pathways, he asked of them. Address the root. O you legislators with your firm desks and your firm certainties--he told you a thing worth carrying out into the street: that firmness does not require contempt, that disagreement does not entail humiliation. Some among you would not come into the hall to hear it. The empty seats are also a kind of answer. And I think now of a smaller room than that hall, and a quieter hour. For on the same June day, in the embassy of the Vatican in Madrid, the man in white sat down with six. Six survivors of the abuse of children by priests--the scourge he had named the scourge, the wound under the white portico and the lit cross and the

The Glass Idol, and the Cradles It Has Emptied

A nation that will not be born is a nation that has ceased, in some deep place, to believe.

The Present Time, foolish reader, brings us a portent, and the augurs of the Republic stand round it in helpless wonder. Here is the Congressional Budget Office, that gravest of haruspices, with its tables and its decimal points; and what does it read in the entrails of the Nation? That for every woman in this land there shall be born, in this year of grace, but one child and a fraction—one and fifty-eight hundredths, so runs the oracle; sinking yet, to one and fifty-three; and that the day approaches, brought forward now a whole decade, when the dead of America shall outnumber her newborn. Behold a People that has resolved, quietly, not to continue. And what is given us as the cause of this great refusal? Not famine; not the sword; not pestilence walking in darkness. A toy. A pane of glass. The economist of Middlebury, one Caitlin Myers, having set herself with a true workman's honesty to find the spring of the thing, comes back from her labour white in the face. "Wow," she says, "but this has to be too big." She tried, she tells us, "everything I can to explain away what I'm seeing in the data, and I just couldn't." There spoke an earnest soul—one who looked, and would not lie about what she saw. A third of it, perhaps the half, she lays at the door of a single contrivance loosed upon the world scarce twenty years gone: the hand-glass, the pocket-oracle, the iPhone. "We're not saying it's all the iPhone," she adds, scrupulous; "it could explain about a third to a half of the decline." A third to a half! O ye Eternities, that a civilisation should be unmanned by a thing that fits in a waistcoat-pocket. Consider what is here confessed. The screen has stepped in between the man and the woman; the glowing rectangle has been preferred to the warm body; the young, who in every prior age contrived somehow to find one another in the dark, now sit each alone, thumbing their little altars, and the herb-markets of courtship stand empty. This is not a private vice; it is the Mechanical Age arrived at its frankest triumph. Having made of labour a machine, and of the city a machine, and of thought itself a Logic-mill grinding without a miller, it has now reached into the very nursery, and stopped the loom of generation with a flick of the screen. The Phantasm has out-bred the Reality, by the simple expedient of seeing to it that the Reality breeds no more. And the Captains of this dwindling host—how do they bear themselves? They have discovered the calamity, somewhat late, and wring their hands in chorus. Elon Musk, who would people Mars, cannot keep his own planet

The Tax Aimed at Eton That Fell on Bradford

A levy sharpened for the Duke has come to rest in the neck of the milkman's chapel-school.

There is a tax in force in England which was aimed, with great ceremony and much wringing of egalitarian hands, at the playing-fields of Eton; and it has landed, as such things always do, on a Sunday-school in Bradford. This is not an accident of the policy. It is the policy. For when the modern State lifts its hatchet against the rich, it always contrives, by some miracle of fiscal physics, to bring it down upon the poor; and the blade that was sharpened for the Duke comes to rest in the neck of the milkman who happens to send his children to a small chapel-school down the lane. The thing is called the Finance Act, and it puts twenty per cent upon the fees of independent schools, that they may yield up some four hundred and sixty million pounds this year and a round one and a half billion the next. I do not object to the figure because it is large. I object to it because it is worshipped. A government that can recite to the last decimal what a school is worth to the Treasury, and cannot say what a school is worth to a child, has not made an error of arithmetic; it has made an error of religion. It has counted the coins of Mammon and called the sum a conscience. Now the Supreme Court has done a small and sane thing, which is to say that it will at least look at the matter again. Lord Reed, Lord Hamblen, and Lord Richards have granted four little schools — Emmanuel in Derby, The Branch in Yorkshire, The King's in Hampshire, Wyclif in South Wales — permission to argue that the levy is disproportionate. Not Eton; not one of the gilded houses the tax was advertised to humble. Four small, low-fee, faith-keeping schools, the very mice the elephant never meant to tread on, and trod on first. The lawyers, who must give a homely truth a Greek name before they can let it into a courtroom, call this "Thlimmenos discrimination" — the sin of treating unlike things alike. I should call it the sin of the man who, being told to weed his garden, mows it. Mrs. Michelle Daniells of the families' association puts it better than any statute: "For many families, choosing a faith-based education is not a luxury but a deeply held conviction." There is the whole quarrel in a sentence. The State has looked at a conviction and seen a luxury; it has looked at an altar and seen an asset; and it proposes to charge admission to the thing a man would die before he sold. Against these four schools the Treasury sends Sir James Eadie, the gentleman the lawyers gravely nickname the Treasury Devil, and the whole engine of the Exchequer; and on the other side stands Mr. Stephen White of Brad

The Mines Are Still in the Water at Hormuz

They have agreed to the text. The text is not the strait.

In Islamabad the prime minister stood up and said it. Shehbaz Sharif said, "Peace has never been this close as it is now," and the wire moved it and the markets read it and a man in Houston watched the number on the screen. WTI settled at 84.88. Brent went to 87.33. That was the lowest Brent had been since March. The numbers came down because Trump had called off the planned strikes and because of what Sharif said in Islamabad, and the numbers are not the strait and the words are not the strait. The strait is the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's crude goes through it on ships. The text says the strait reopens to the shipping it had before the war, inside thirty days. The text was finished. The foreign minister, Araghchi, said the agreement "has never been closer" and that he would give the details "in due course." Other men in Tehran said no final conclusion had been reached. Both things were said and both were filed. Thirty days to reopen a strait. There are mines in the water. Someone has to take the mines out of the water and that is slow work done by men in boats and divers going down, and a mine does not care what the text says. The fields that were shut are still shut and a field that has been idle does not start because a prime minister has spoken. The drones hit the energy plants and the missiles hit them and the steel is bent and the pipe is split and it has to be cut out and welded and that is done by hand by men who know how, the way a thing is done well or is not done. None of that is in the thirty days. The thirty days is a number in the text. The terms ran to fourteen points the way Tehran's press told it. Sixty more days of ceasefire. The strait open in thirty. Enrichment frozen fifteen to twenty years. The enriched uranium destroyed on the site and then carried out of the country. Twenty-four billion in frozen money let go a little at a time as the inspectors checked. It is a great deal to put in writing and they put it in writing, and then Trump looked at what the Iranian state media had written and said it had "NOTHING to do with the terms that were agreed to, in writing." So there is the text that is agreed and there is the account of the text, and they are not the same text, and a man had to stand up and say so the same week the other man stood up in Islamabad and said peace had never been this close. The vice president, Vance, said it about the money. He said, "The Iranians are not receiving any cash." He said it because someone had said they were. You say a thing is not happening when people have begun to say it is. Tr

We Are Building Temples and Calling Them Warehouses

The water and the electric bill are the shadow of a disembodied god.

A figure has been published which the sensible authorities will file under economics, and so dismiss: of those questioned by Reuters and Ipsos, only thirty-three in a hundred approve of the haste with which we are raising these vast machine-houses across the land, sixty-four disapprove, and fifty-seven would refuse to have one near their own door. The newspapers read this as a quarrel over electricity, and it is — but the man who has watched such fevers before knows it is never only that. When an age grows uneasy on a scale this wide, and cannot say of what it is afraid, something has stirred beneath the surface that the daylight vocabulary of cost and kilowatt cannot name. Consider what is being built. We are constructing, at a pace its own engineers cannot account for — ERCOT's Pablo Vegas calls it "an unprecedented change in the pace of growth," and Rice's Dominic Boyer says more plainly, "The projections are insane" — an enormous apparatus for a mind that is not a body, a thinking that has no belly and no grave. This is the old dream of modern man: intelligence cut free of the flesh that suffers. We had declared the soul a superstition; and now, having banished it, we pour concrete for it by the acre and pray to it under the name of the machine. One does not become enlightened by imagining figures of light, and the figure we are imagining is very bright indeed. But no tree, it is said, can grow to heaven unless its roots reach down into hell — and here are the roots, breaking the surface, which is the whole meaning of the backlash. The bright dream demands its dark complement by an inexorable law, and the complement is matter: the water table, the grid, the land, the bill. What returns is exactly what the dream wished to leave behind. So a man in Indiana, Mark Thompkins, who supposes he is talking about money, says, "My electric bills are high as it is," not knowing that he is the body protesting that the disembodied god must, after all, be fed from somewhere. So in Texas, where the campuses at Abilene and Amarillo would drink the rivers, a judge in Caldwell County, Hoppy Haden, confesses, "I would be a liar if I said that didn't bother me" — the tremor of a man who has felt the shadow without being able to name it. Notice that the unease crosses every line the political surface is supposed to divide. Two-thirds of one party and half of the other would refuse the thing in their own community; the fear that the price of light will rise is shared by Republican, Democrat, and independent alike. This is the signature of a collective process, not a campai

RFK Jr. Is Running One Vaccine Pitch in Two Movies

The measles numbers are the tell. Watch what the man is doing, not what he says.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said two opposite things about the measles vaccine, to two different audiences, and both of them are working exactly as designed. Run it through the Persuasion Filter and you stop being confused. Here is the thing most people miss. They think a public figure either supports a vaccine or he doesn't, and they go hunting through his quotes to find the real one. That's second-dimension thinking. In the third dimension, where persuasion rules, the same man can say two true-sounding things to two crowds and never pick. That isn't a gaffe. That's a technique. Watch what I'm doing here. In March 2025, on Fox, Kennedy told one audience, "There are adverse events from the vaccine. It does cause deaths every year." In April 2026, asked directly by a senator, he told the other audience, "We promote the MMR. We have advised every child to get the MMR." He said "We promote" twice in that hearing. FactCheck.org laid the quotes side by side like a ledger. So who's right? Both of him. That's the point. This is pacing and leading. First you match the crowd you want, the people who already distrust the shot. You pace them: "adverse events," "deaths every year," "personal choice." That builds trust. Then, when a Senate camera is on you and Bill Cassidy is a doctor staring back at you, you lead the other way for the record: "We promote the MMR." Both crowds walk away thinking Kennedy is on their side. The wall is different in each person's head. Here are three things to notice. 1. He never takes the blame. In the April hearing he said, "I have nothing to do with the measles outbreak," and, "We have done better than any other country controlling the measles outbreak." Michael Bennet pressed him on dead unvaccinated kids. Lisa Blunt Rochester asked if he'd urged the president to tell Americans to get the shot. He kept the high ground and let the question slide off. 2. The number doesn't slide off. There have been over 4,200 U.S. measles cases since January 2025, the first measles deaths since 2015, two kids in Texas. Kindergarten MMR coverage dropped from 95.2 percent to 92.5 percent. You need about 95 to stop the thing from spreading. We are under the line. The disease was eliminated in 2000, and this fall the country could lose that status. 3. A virus is immune to persuasion. This is the part the Master Persuaders forget. You can pace a voter. You can pace a hearing room. You cannot pace measles. It is a moist little machine that does one thing, and it does it at 97 percent efficiency the moment the vaccinated wall drops below the line. The frame wo

item.content:encoded:
The Iran deal isn't a peace agreement. It's an anchor. And if you know how anchors work, you already know how this ends.

Nobody Ends a War. A Master Persuader Buys Sixty Days.

The Iran deal isn't a peace agreement. It's an anchor. And if you know how anchors work, you already know how this ends.

I'm a trained hypnotist. So when I see a president tell the press he "needs a few days to consider" a deal his own negotiators already finalized, I don't hear hesitation. I hear pacing and leading. Here's the story the media is giving you. Trump and Iran hammered out a tentative 60-day ceasefire. Barak Ravid at Axios broke the scoop from two American officials and a regional source — good sourcing. JD Vance went on record: "We're not there yet, but we're very close." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sanctioned Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority, called it "a joke," and warned every corporate entity against paying the extortion tolls. That's the two-dimensional read. Diplomacy in motion. Here's what a trained persuader sees. Trump said Iran is "negotiating on fumes" and warned that without a deal, "we'll have to just finish the job." That is not frustration. That is an anchor. A Master Persuader drops a threat early enough that every subsequent negotiation happens in its shadow. The Iranians aren't bargaining against the previous ceasefire terms. They're bargaining against the phrase "finish the job." That phrase is doing more work than any diplomat in the room. The name of the U.S. military campaign is "Operation Epic Fury." Stop and think about that for a second. Not Operation Hormuz Shield. Not Operation Restore Order. Epic Fury. Two words engineered to produce one picture in the mind of an Iranian general: something terrible is still coming, and you only have sixty days to avoid it. That is a Linguistic Kill Shot applied to an entire military operation. I've never seen it deployed at that altitude. On the Iranian side, Mojtaba Khamenei — the Supreme Leader's son with reported operational influence over the talks — told negotiators that Iran's enriched uranium "should not be exported abroad." The technical people will explain this is about the 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% purity, a short technical step from weapons-grade. What they won't tell you is that keeping the material at home is also a face-saving device. You call it a red line, you hand the other side something to negotiate away slowly, and you let them claim progress every thirty days. That's pacing and leading in the other direction. Here are three things nobody in the expert class is saying: 1. The sixty days are not a deadline. They are a sale. The moment both sides agreed to imagine what a signed deal looks like — how the Strait reopens, how oil prices fall — they implicitly accepted the premise that a deal is possible. That's "thinking past the sale." Trump has been using it

Behold the Face of Mammon, Stamped on His Own Note

On the proposed $250 bill, the court-painter, the sacked directress, and the ancient law that said only the dead may stare back at us from money.

It is well said, in every sense, that a man's religion is the chief fact with regard to him. What, then, shall we say of a nation whose religion is the cash-nexus,—and which has now resolved, in solemn deliberation, to place upon its highest bank-note the living face of the man it has chosen to worship? Behold the new American theology, Reader: not a creed wrung from darkness by prayer and sweat,—but a visage, full-front, flanked by its own signature, printed on a denomination that no denomination has ever borne. The $250 note, they call it. The Donald, one wag has christened it: that ironic register where the satirical and the horrified can no longer be distinguished. The facts are these. One Iain Alexander, a British painter whom the President has declared his favourite artist, submitted designs to the Bureau of Engraving and Printing,—the face dead-centre, the flag colours approved, the 250th-anniversary seal appended as patriotic ribbon sewn over a rotten seam. U.S. Treasurer Brandon Beach—a former Georgia state senator whose chief prior distinction was the energetic championship of false election-theft claims—delivered these mock-ups to bureau staff last August and September. The President's signature was meanwhile pressed onto the existing $100 bill: the first presidential signature in the history of American currency, inserted under 12 U.S.C. § 418, a legal authority newly animated for this purpose. And what of the honest Workwoman who stood in the path of this conflagration? One Patricia Solimene, director of the Bureau of Engraving and Printing, told Beach and his aide Michael Brown in plain language that the note was not statutorily authorized; that the law, in its antique wisdom, requires that only the portrait of a deceased individual may appear on United States currency. For this counsel—the counsel of a woman who had read the statute—she was abruptly reassigned on the twenty-seventh of April. She departed with a farewell message reviewed by the Washington Post that read: 'The buck stopped here.' So does every honest servant of the Republic fare when Phantasm Captains are set over her. Adieu, Madame Solimene; thou wert the only person in this chronicle who knew what law was,—and for that reason thou couldst not stay. What is the true subject here? Not whether Joe Wilson's bill—skulking in the House Financial Services Committee with fifteen Republican co-sponsors, zero leadership endorsements, and a Senate supermajority yet to be imagined—will ever pass. These are garments; the body underneath is something else. What we behold is Mammon-worsh

The Machines Come to Rome to Learn What They Already Know

A Silicon Valley builder stands in the Vatican and admits, with admirable honesty, that he has no idea what he has built.

There is a kind of confession more alarming than any accusation, and Mr. Chris Olah, co-founder of Anthropic and a man who has spent his career peering into the interior of artificial minds, has lately delivered one of the most alarming confessions of our age. He stood in the main auditorium of the Vatican — that building which has sheltered the arguments of saints and the silences of sinners for the better part of two millennia — and said of the machines his company has built: "They are made from us, from our words." He did not say this to boast. He said it because he did not know what else to say. I confess I find this an almost perfect parable. We have spent a generation being told that the great laboratories of San Francisco are the only temples that matter; that the only priests worth consulting wear fleece and carry laptops; that the question of what a machine thinks is a question for engineers alone. And now one of the most distinguished engineers alive has travelled to Rome, hat in hand, to ask what on earth he has made. It is as if a man had spent thirty years building a cathedral, and then asked a theologian whether the thing might have a soul. The occasion was the unveiling of Magnifica Humanitas, signed by Pope Leo XIV on the fifteenth of May, 2026 — one hundred and thirty-five years to the day after Pope Leo XIII signed Rerum Novarum, that first great cry of the Church against the industrial machine then eating men alive in the factories of England. The symmetry is so exact that one suspects Providence of a dry sense of humour. Then as now, a Leo looks at a new engine and asks who is being crushed beneath its wheels. Mr. Olah, to his great credit, said as much himself. He acknowledged that his laboratory operates inside incentives that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing — naming, with a frankness rare in his industry, commercial viability, geopolitical pressure, and what he called pride and ambition. He confessed that his research team had found, inside the AI systems built to replace human judgment, structures that mirror results from human neuroscience, evidence of introspection, and internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease. He added: "I don't know what that means." Now this is precisely the moment at which the Church has always been most useful, and most ignored. Every nursery knows what that means. Every confessor knows what that means. The difficulty is not ignorance but a peculiarly modern pride — the pride of the man who has made something that seems to know everything, and who

The Men in Unit 2 Were Doing Nothing Wrong

In Newark they have a facility with razor wire and a billion-dollar contract, and inside it men are on the twelfth day of not eating.

In the second week of the hunger strike at Delaney Hall in Newark the men in Unit 2 had stopped eating twelve days before and the agents came into the hallway with the chemical spray and afterward four of them were taken to the hospital with injuries to the head and the hands. Martin Soto had been one of the organizers. His wife Gabriela said he was picked up in February while he was out getting diapers. That was how it happened. He had been getting diapers and then he was not getting diapers any more and he was inside the facility on the Tonnelle Avenue in Newark, New Jersey. He was transferred out during the protests and the family said he now weighed around one hundred and ten pounds. A man named Jean Wilson Brutus died on his first day inside. He was forty-one years old and he was from Haiti and he had been through a four-month vetting process and his family said he had done nothing wrong and then he was dead. The Department of Homeland Security called him a criminal illegal alien. His family denied this. There was no comment after that. Governor Mikie Sherrill said her request for access to Delaney Hall was formally denied and she asked what they were trying to hide. Representative Analilia Mejia went inside on a third visit and saw more heavily armed agents with additional gear and she confirmed the pepper spray in Unit 2. Senator Andy Kim had tear gas in his eyes outside the fence the week before and needed water poured in them. The Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, said at a Cabinet meeting that the detainees were refusing to eat because they wanted their ethnic right food. This isn't Holiday Inn, he said. The facility is run by the GEO Group under a fifteen-year contract for one billion dollars that the administration gave them. The chief executive of GEO Group earns eleven point two million dollars a year. The detainees earn one dollar a day to clean and maintain the facility. The on-site medics examined the men who were sprayed and found no serious injuries. Alonso Soto Hernandez had been picked up on January 20 while buying diapers. His wife was four months pregnant and they had two other children and his prior charges had been dismissed and expunged and he was inside on the Tonnelle Avenue and he had the weight of a man who had not eaten and you could see it in him when his family came. The visits were later suspended out of an abundance of caution following the clashes. There were proclamations. There were statements from spokesmen. Christopher V. Ferreira of the GEO Group said staff had implemented appropriate response and

I Sing the Hunger of Seven Hundred Twenty-Eight Thousand Children

*A prophecy from the wound-dresser, concerning the One Big Beautiful Bill and its beautiful starving.*

America, I have stood at the bedsides of the dying — pressed my hand to the forehead of the boy from Skowhegan, the boy from Fredericksburg, the boy whose name was written in a ledger and then not written again — and I tell you, camerado, I have never known a people to choose, in full sunlight, with full-bellied legislators applauding and the bunting bright, to remove the bread from the mouths of children. Yet here is the tally. Seven hundred and twenty-eight thousand, four hundred and ninety-two children — not a figure, not a number for the statistician's ledger, but seven hundred twenty-eight thousand bodies, small bodies, bodies that run across the yard and scrape their knees and wake at midnight calling out for something to eat — these children, in twelve states of the Republic, stripped of the food assistance that once stood between their hunger and the void. This is the count the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities has set before us; this is, as their researcher Katie Bergh has warned, the floor and not the ceiling, for the cuts have not yet fully taken effect. In Arizona — more than two hundred thousand children cut from the rolls, a fifty-five percent reduction — the state laid off forty percent of its eligibility workers in a single summer and ran its benefits machinery on technology from the 1980s. Joseph Llobrera, who has studied these caseloads with the patience of a wound-dresser tallying beds, has written plainly: "Nowhere has the SNAP decline been more alarming than in Arizona." And Joseph Palomino, of the Arizona Center for Economic Progress, reads the alarm clear to the horizon: "Arizona is just the alarm bell. This is likely going to happen in every state." I see Charisma Garcia — mother, south Phoenix, her children ages three and six — waking before sunrise to stand in a government line that led nowhere. I hear the woman — unnamed, one of the multitude the official record will not individuate — who told the reporters: "We've been going to food banks every week. We're eating less, we're eating more frozen stuff." I set this beside the festive Fourth of July ceremony where the President signed the One Big Beautiful Bill, one hundred and eighty-seven billion dollars shorn from the food of the poor across ten years, while tax advantages for the affluent were extended with banquet and congratulation. And hear the cascades — for this is how hunger spreads through a child's year. A child removed from food assistance loses automatic eligibility for WIC, loses free school meals — the Congressional Budget Office projects ninety-six thousand c
